items.lbText:
A record breaking IPO has raised billions for the AI frontier lab – but experts say the coming months could prove bumpy, as the industry faces a variety of challenges

Anthropic closes first day of public trading at $1.3tn valuation after largest-ever IPO

In the end, Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO more than lived up to the hype. The market’s embrace of one of the AI industry’s most talked about companies has resulted in the maker of the Claude chatbot becoming one of the world’s most valuable firms after just one day of trading.

With many of the company’s founders, investors and employees now worth billions of dollars – and demand for the company’s stock remaining resilient – attention now turns to the stability of the wider market, and the global headwinds that experts say could threaten the AI industry over the coming months.

Here’s a rundown of what we can gather after a big day for Anthropic and the AI industry

“The blockbuster Anthropic launch is a critical step in reassuring the market about the potential for AI, but ​it’s really just the beginning,” said Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.

We still need to see ‌what happens with OpenAI, how the Nvidia situation evolves , how ‌the political climate for data centres shapes up, and what the historical performance for Anthropic proves to be before we’ll get any real sense of stability.”

In early trading on Friday, Asian stocks plunged by up to 4%, suggesting Anthropic’s debut has done little to settle nerves on trading floors.

According to reports demand for Anthropic shares was about six times what the company was able to offer, an incredible result for a company founded in 2021.

Started by a number of former OpenAI employees, Anthropic initially lagged behind its rival frontier lab, but analysts say its focus on building software for business and programming clients has helped to position it as one of the market leaders.

That breakneck growth has left investors stunned; from fledgling start-up six years ago, Anthropic is now worth more than US stock market stalwarts Walmart, JP Morgan, Visa and ExxonMobil.

The speed of its growth is reflected in its revenue: according to its investor prospectus, Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn in revenue for all of 2025.

But Anthropic has also lost an enormous amount of money. In the first half of 2026, the company reported losses of $80bn, though that was largely due to a one-off charge. Losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. The firm has said its costs will balloon as it invests further in datacentres.

The IPO hands Anthropic a pool of new cash to make those investments, but with promises to spend about $900bn on datacentre infrastructure over the next two decades, experts say their debt is likely to rise even further.

Newly minted Anthropic investors will also have to contend with rising public sentiment against AI.

Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei has been among the loudest voices pointing out the dangers that the products he and his rivals are developing may pose to humanity. He has called for a slowdown on the development of the most advanced AI models after employees expressed concerns that they were being built irresponsibly.

Across the US, opposition to AI companies has manifested in protests against local datacentre plans , with a number of municipalities and states voting for bans or restrictions on them at the recent midterm elections.

US economic growth is inextricably tied to the booming AI sector, and in particular the vast investments in datacentres that power programmes like Claude and ChatGPT. One estimate from Harvard professor Jason Furman suggested “investment in information processing equipment and software” accounted for 92% of the US’s GDP growth in the first half of 2025.

Any slowdown in that expenditure on datacentres could therefore have far-reaching consequences for Anthropic – and the global economy.

Anthropic’s leaders are also likely looking ahead to the changes to government next year, when Democrats take over both chambers of Congress after securing large majorities in the midterm elections.

Senior Democrats have already suggested that tech companies could face a regulatory crackdown over the dangers that advanced AI models pose, and over the volatility that AI IPOs could introduce into the economy.

Last month Democrat Elizabeth Warren, a senior member of the Senate banking committee, appeared to signal such moves, telling Amodei in a letter that Anthropic’s IPO “could inject extreme volatility and risk into the financial system, which threatens to undermine Americans’ economic security.”

The fact that Anthropic is burning through cash and requires an insatiable stream of capital to feed its growth is not a reason to expose everyday Americans to the company’s risks in our public stock markets … Swings in Anthropic’s share price have the potential to roil the broader markets on day one.”

Jensen Huang – the former CEO of Nvidia, the most important company in providing the advanced chips that power AI – is due to appear before Congress next month. He’ll be answering questions about his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, a scandal that has resulted in the loss of one of Silicon Valley’s key figures and sparked bipartisan national security concerns.

Earlier this year Anthropic’s chief rival, OpenAI, decided to postpone its initial offering until 2027. Experts say that Anthropic’s market reception and the movements in its share price will act as a signal to others in the industry over what the appetite for another large AI IPO will be.

Earlier this week, Open AI CEO Sam Altman said his company will go ahead with the IPO next year, even in the face of increased volatility.…

The company counts physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among its guiding lights

The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations.

The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price.

Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, which he co-founded with Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price.

At the closing price of $97.17, the combined co-founders’ stakes had fallen in value to just over $160bn at around $23bn each. The Sound Ventures stake was worth about $8.75bn.

Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market , though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.

Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes that it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI.

Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist.

In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”.

Anthropic’s San Francisco-born chief executive was educated at Stanford and Princeton universities. He worked at the Chinese tech firm Baidu and then at Google before joining OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT and now Anthropic’s arch-rival, where he had a key position as vice-president of research.

In 2020, Amodei left OpenAI, and it has been widely reported that his departure was due to conflicting views over safety. “It is incredibly unproductive to try and argue with someone else’s vision,” he said years later.

AI safety remains a major concern for Amodei. He called for a slowdown in AI development in September after the resignation of an employee who cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity and triggered a wave of concern about the existential threat posed by the technology.

Amodei is also blunt about the potential impact of AI on jobs, claiming that AI could eliminate half of all white-collar jobs by the end of the decade.

Amodei, Dario’s sister, began her career in politics, working in Congress and on a congressional campaign, before switching to tech and taking a job at Stripe, the payment processor. She moved to OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic with her brother. She leads teams on AI model safety and alignment , making sure AI systems adhere to human aims and values.

Like other Anthropic employees and co-founders, Amodei is tied to the EA movement. She is married to one of its major donors, Holden Karnofsky, who co-founded GiveWell and the major grant-giving organisation Open Philanthropy.

This Brighton-born former journalist has been catapulted into the list of richest Britons with the Anthropic flotation. His paper wealth of approximately $26.6bn (£20.3bn) compares with £38bn for the London-based Hinduja brothers and puts him above the £18.2bn fortune of the Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne and Manchester United’s co-owner Jim Ratcliffe, who is worth £15.2bn. Clark leads the Anthropic Institute, a thinktank devoted to researching the social implications of advanced AI.

In a lecture at Oxford University this year, Clark predicted that an AI system will work with humans to make a Nobel prize-winning discovery within 12 months, and that tradespeople will be helped by bipedal robots within two years. He added that it would be better if humans could slow the development of the technology “to give ourselves more time as a species” to deal with the implications of its powers.

Anthropic’s chief science officer received a PhD in theoretical particle physics from Harvard before working as a researcher at OpenAI, then co-founding Anthropic. He is known for his work on scaling laws – the idea that AI models grow smarter and more powerful in proportion with the resources that are spent on training them.

In an interview with the Guardian last year, Kaplan focused on the major AI safety concern that animates much of Anthropic’s work – the power and potential risk of AI systems that can improve themselves. Creating such systems would be “the ultimate risk,” he said.

Anthropic’s chief compute officer, who is in charge of the company’s use and procurement of datacentres, was a senior engineer at OpenAI. Given his job title, he is unsurprisingly supportive of a divisive topic in US politics: whether to build more datacentres. Speaking in September, Brown praised Donald Trump’s social media post stating “let data reign”.…

Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask

R oll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company .

From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees .

And, to be fair, it wasn’t nailed-on that the show would go so swimmingly. There was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed – or Jensened – by the soap opera at Nvidia . More generally, there was a worry that the AI bubble, if that’s what it is, could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go.

Anthropic, though, has set records by raising $107bn. It is an extraordinary sum, especially for a business founded five years ago. At the listing price, Anthropic was valued at $1.5tn. When shares began trading at £111.50, its market capitalisation was up to $2tn. Only 14 months ago, it raised money at a valuation of a “mere” $183bn .

The feat, though, is not wholly inexplicable. Some $26bn of the listing proceeds were virtually in the bag, thanks to the cornerstone placement to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. That assembly of AI and AI-adjacent names fed worries about the industry’s circular financing.

But, on the other hand, every fund manager knew he or she would be betting against the crowd by saying no. Momentum can carry a stock a long way, even before the index funds and index-hugging funds are obliged to buy (Nasdaq entry will be quick; the S&P 500 will take at least a year).

Take a step back, though, and ask whether Anthropic – loss-making and with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish – can possibly be worth $1.5tn-plus.

The short, and unhelpful, answer is that virtually any valuation could be made to sound plausible if you believe, first, that AI is a generational technology that will be adopted at never-seen-before speed and, second, that “frontier” pioneering firms, of which Anthropic is the leader, will capture an outsized slice of the commercial value for years and years.

Consider the assumptions behind that thesis, however. Can Anthropic really improve from $50bn-ish of revenue this year to $600bn in 2030, which is roughly what tech analysts have pencilled in? Given the current rate of growth, perhaps it can. But sustaining the pace, or something like it, for another 16 quarters simply won’t be straightforward or mechanical.

What is the real level of demand from corporate users for frontier models? Nobody doubts that AI adoption is still in the early stage, but does everybody need the finest product from Anthropic’s Claude suite? Already executives grumble that their IT budgets are finite and that nine-month-old versions, or cheaper “open weight” models from rivals, do the job for basic work. Lasting pricing power in AI is simply unclear. “Commoditisation risk”, in the jargon, could be the next year’s valuation debate.

Then there is the investment bill to make it all happen – $900bn of spending commitments were detailed in the prospectus for computing power and infrastructure. The listing proceeds help, as does the visibility and credibility that comes with being on a public market. But debt, not just equity, will be a crucial part of this story.

“Obviously, at some point in the future we’re hoping to be investment grade,” said co-founder Dario Amodei as trading in the shares started. You bet: the price at which Anthropic borrows matters fundamentally.

Away from the party atmosphere, the European Central Bank has its eye on financial stability in the eurozone. This week, it issued one of those fuddy-duddy reminders about how much capital is being bet on the AI revolution , and how little transparency there is around the funding of hyperscalers and other suppliers to the boom.

“Big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than $4tn as of the second quarter of 2026,” its report said, warning of “historical parallels with the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles”.

It is not the only one to see warning signs. Anthropic is an astonishingly successful company already and is plainly at the forefront of a significant technological shift. But it has been listed in an environment that looks – to most of us who remember the late 1990s and the subsequent bust – to have bubbly characteristics. AI technology, like the internet, is gamechanging. But it doesn’t mean today’s share prices are right.

items.lbText:
Citizens Advice criticises company for failing to meet Ofcom requirements while reporting increased revenue

Royal Mail has been accused of offering a “pot luck service” to consumers as it looks likely to miss first-class delivery targets for the fourth consecutive year.

The postal service, whose parent company was bought for £3.6bn by the Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský last year, is meant to deliver 90% of its first-class post by the next working day and 95% of second-class post within three working days according to targets set by the regulator, Ofcom.

But it delivered only 82.5% of first-class mail within target in the second quarter of this year, down from 85% in the first quarter. Second-class deliveries slipped to 87.2% arriving within three working days, compared with 91.4% in the previous quarter.

On Thursday, Royal Mail said it did not expect to meet its targets until next April. It last met its first-class delivery target in 2017, before they were temporarily suspended during the pandemic.

Tom MacInnes, the director of policy at the charity Citizens Advice, said: “Putting a letter in a postbox shouldn’t be like rolling a dice to see if it arrives on time.

“But that’s the pot luck service consumers get with Royal Mail.”

Royal Mail has been fined a total of £37m since 2023 for missing delivery targets set by Ofcom. In June, the regulator launched an investigation into the company for the missed targets, saying it would investigate whether the company was prioritising parcel delivery over letters, a practice alleged by whistleblowers and unions but denied by the company.

The postal service is preparing for its busiest period of the year, beginning with the Black Friday shopping event in the run-up to Christmas.

“It is not really Black Friday any more, it’s like a Black Friday month,” said Martin Seidenberg, the chief executive of Royal Mail’s parent company International Distribution Services (IDS). He added that it was “already quite busy in the network”, but said “we are ready”.

Royal Mail said on Thursday it had hired an additional 22,000 seasonal workers and was ready for “a very busy Christmas”.

On the same day, IDS reported a 6.3% rise in revenue to £6.85bn in the six months to 27 September. Royal Mail’s revenue rose 3.9% to £4.13bn.

The number of letters being sent through Royal Mail has more than halved in the past decade, falling from about 20bn to 6.7bn. The number of addresses it serves has gone up by 4m in the same period.

The company has continued to miss performance targets despite Ofcom giving it permission last year to downgrade its universal service obligation . This has meant a reduction in second-class deliveries to alternate weekdays, with no second-class deliveries on Saturdays.

In April, Royal Mail faced criticism for raising the price of a first-class stamp by 10p , or 6%, to £1.80, and a second-class stamp by 4p, or 5%, to 91p. It blamed the increases on the “continued rise in the cost of delivery for every letter”.

The business has announced plans to cut up to 2,500 jobs as part of an effort to restructure, with a focus on head office and “support function roles”. It last made a big round of cuts in 2022 , when it said it was looking to eliminate up to 10,000 roles, including 6,000 full-time frontline jobs.

A spokesperson said: “Royal Mail is broadly on track to deliver against its quality of service improvement plan with first-class next-working-day performance up 9.1 percentage points on last year and ahead of the trajectory set out in the plan.

“Taking into account the emergency exemption to regulatory quality of service targets during the pandemic, Royal Mail has missed its regulatory targets for the last four years.”

CEO of Cambridge-based firm viewed as leading contender to replace co-founder Jensen Huang according to reports

Nvidia’s headhunters have reportedly approached the chief executive of the Cambridge-based chip company Arm, in its search for a new leader after Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit.

Heidrick & Struggles, the recruiting firm hired by the company’s board, has started contacting potential candidates, according to Bloomberg.

It reported that Rene Haas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, is among those approached.

Nvidia is searching for a replacement for Huang, one of the firm’s founders, who resigned last week after he admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of spying for China .

Haas, 64, is viewed as the leading contender for the top job at Nvidia , having previously worked at the $3.6tn (£2.8tn) company for seven years as the general manager of its computing products.

Reports suggest that other potential candidates include: Ian Buck, an Nvidia vice-president; Lisa Su, AMD’s chief executive; and Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer.

Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Nvidia, Apple, Samsung and Qualcomm. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including more than 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech firm headquartered in Britain, now valued at $196bn.

Haas told a tech conference in Austin on Wednesday that Huang was “a legend”. “What he built at Nvidia is historic,” he said. “You don’t have many champions like that.”

Nvidia has sought to curb speculation that Huang could return to his role, after he said on Tuesday that he would be willing to come back.

He wrote in a statement: “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

It came after US president, Donald Trump, and Silicon Valley insiders – including Elon Musk, prominent venture capitalists and the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick – called for Huang’s reinstatement.

However, the Nvidia chair, Harvey Jones, confirmed at the company’s quarterly earnings results this week that the board “ does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO ”.

Jones said that “while this was an unexpected transition … the board is proactively dealing with the consequences”.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and presented the financial results on Tuesday, which showed that its quarterly revenue had doubled from the same period a year ago to $115.84bn.

Huang agreed on Tuesday to appear before the House of Representatives foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the intelligence committee for transcribed interviews in early December. Nvidia also faces an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its business in China, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.

Nvidia and Arm were approached for comment.

Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier brings account base up to 6m after purchase of pay-as-you-go supplier

EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita.

Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed.

The pair will continue to serve their customers independently until the deal concludes. Utilita customers will be contacted about any changes to their service.

After the deal, EDF has promised to continue to operate from Utilita’s headquarters near Southampton which is the base for about 600of Utilita’s employees.

EDF, which is owned by the French state, set out the takeover plans a year after it completed a deal to take on 47,000 standard credit accounts from Utilita which said it hoped to sharpen its focus on smart pay-as-you-go customers.

The deal is likely to have helped bolster Utilita’s financial position, which briefly fell short of the industry regulator Ofgem’s tougher new financial resilience tests in an industry assessment in September 2025.

Utilita confirmed that it was one of five suppliers which had failed to meet Ofgem’s financial rules last year, but said it was able to comply with the standards within months of the regulator’s red flag.

For EDF, the deal will help to bolster its business as most large suppliers continue to lose customers to smaller rivals. EDF lost about 280,000 customer accounts in the year after July 2025, while British Gas, Scottish Power and E.ON Next were also losing customers. Octopus Energy , the country’s largest supplier, is the only big energy company which has continued to grow its market share.

Utilita was founded in 2003 as a specialist prepay energy supplier, and became the first supplier to install a smart meter in 2008.

Its pioneering approach to smart metering helped the company to modernise pay-as-you-go energy by allowing customers to top-up via an app, website, or by phone rather than visit a corner shop or post office to pay for credit on a plastic card or key.

Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF’s UK business, said Utilita would bring “further expertise” to the supplier, marking “a significant step” in EDF’s ambition to grow its UK customer business.

“Together, we will have the scale and skills to keep developing services and support for the households who rely on us,” Rossi said.

Bill Bullen, the founder of Utilita, said the deal would ensure that Utilita could continue to provide “best-in-class smart prepay solutions to Britain’s households”.

Last month, German energy group E.ON Next completed a deal to buy struggling UK rival Ovo after the deal was approved by Britain’s competition watchdog.

The deal comes as households prepare for a sharp rise in energy bills this winter. On Wednesday, the consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast the quarterly industry price cap would jump 26% from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.

items.lbText:
Job cuts to exclude shop floor, aircraft maintenance and trainees but move prompts calls for more orders to support British defence giant

BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, triggering calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor.

The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”.

The cuts represent about 2% of its 50,000 strong workforce in the UK, which includes about 18,500 in its air business and about 1,000 in its head office in London. They will be made through voluntary redundancies and will exclude people working on the shop floor, aircraft maintenance at RAF bases and early career trainees.

A spokesperson for BAE said the cuts represented the “next stage of our ongoing focus on enhancing our agility and competitiveness, so we can help to maximise the value of every pound our customers spend on defence.

“We recognise that this news may be unsettling for our people and we’re focused on achieving potential workforce reductions through a voluntary process,” they said.

BAE last year received an order for 20 Typhoon fighter jets from Turkey, in a deal announced at the factory by Keir Starmer. However, that order is thought to provide only two years of work at the Lancashire factories – not enough to sustain jobs until production starts on the next generation of fighters. BAE will lead production of the sixth-generation Tempest fighter in an alliance with Italy and Japan.

A source with knowledge of the matter said that the job cuts were linked to uncertainty over the Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet programme , more than cost-cutting.

The move comes even as BAE has benefited from a boom in defence spending since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, the company told its investors it had secured £33bn in orders so far this year and that it expected further contracts before the end of 2026. It also raised its free cashflow guidance for its financial year by 10%, from about £2bn to £3bn.

Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the union Unite, warned that there would not be a manufacturing industry left in the UK “if the government doesn’t start making critical decisions”.

“To stop the erosion of defence jobs and get the growth we need, the government needs to announce contracts for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) immediately,” she said.

BAE unveiled the uncrewed CCA – which is named Brontanax – at the Farnborough International airshow in July.

Andrew Snowden, a Conservative MP in Lancashire where BAE has two air manufacturing hubs, echoed Graham’s call for more government support.

He told the Lancashire Post: “The government should act now to support BAE by placing orders for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft, giving skilled workers and the supply chain here in Lancashire a clear pipeline of work.”

It comes with the government also under pressure to reach a decision on its Skynet military satellite replacement. American weapons maker Lockheed Martin was thought to be the Ministry of Defence’s preferred choice, but ministers have delayed the choice after Unite argued it would lead to UK job cuts at rival Airbus’s existing factories.

An MoD spokesperson said: “We know that any potential voluntary redundancies can cause concerns and our thoughts are with those potentially affected.

“This government is delivering the biggest boost in defence spending since the cold ar, having already agreed £4bn worth of investments since July.

“This includes awarding BAE a £708m contract extension to lead the Global Combat Air Programme developments and supporting the £8bn contract to supply Turkey with 20 Typhoon jets last year, which sustains 6,000 jobs at two BAE sites.”

items.lbText:
UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash

A ndrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera .

Bailey and his senior managers believe they can modernise the Bank’s Grade I-listed structure and interiors while 3,500 staff are still busy at work on site.

By the summer of 2028, 1,400 Bank staff who work in a nearby office at 20 Moorgate will be relocated to Threadneedle Street, have taken voluntary redundancy or have been offered an alternative job in a new outpost in Leeds, also being refurbished.

It appears a unique project for Britain’s struggling building trade: overhaul a site with a globally recognised exterior; preserve its Roman mosaic floors, stone columns and vaulted, ornate ceilings while keeping exact floorplans under wraps, for fear of terror attacks.

The Bank itself began in rented premises in 1694, moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734. Nicknamed the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street after a satirical cartoon of William Pitt the Younger , it has been refashioned and remodelled – first by Sir John Soane between 1788 and 1833 and then again in the 1920s when the interior was largely demolished and rebuilt.

The building is owned by the Bank, which was given independence to set interest rates by Gordon Brown in 1997 , and, after the 2008 financial crash, it was later handed responsibility for regulating the banking sector by George Osborne.

Cash to fund the scheme will come from an estimated £100m of savings each year for three years that the Bank says will accrue from 450 redundancies and other cost savings. As one member of Bank staff told the Guardian: “It’s like there is a leaving party every week.”

What the Bank wants to avoid is a repeat of the delays and cost overruns that dogged the Federal Reserve in Washington, which led to Trump threatening the US central bank with court action.

Over the life of the Fed’s renovation project, construction costs have soared. The initial budget of $921m (£696m) in February 2020 was revised several times before December 2024, when it hit $2bn. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is now expected to run until December 2027. The final cost is likely to be nearer $2.5bn.

The Bank’s scheme is on a much smaller scale, and pales against the possible £60bn it will cost to renovate the Palace of Westminster . It is more akin to the £80m Elizabeth Tower restoration.

What Bailey will want to avoid is joining the Elizabeth Tower, which houses Big Ben, as the subject of parliamentary scrutiny after its budget doubled and then rose by a further 20% , giving ammunition to critics who have long accused the Bank of mishandling its core purpose of helping to manage the economy by setting interest rates at the appropriate level.

The Bank project was first announced in July 2025 and work was due to start this month, but it was only in October, with a month to spare, that the construction company Sir Robert McAlpine was awarded the building contract.

Described as an “incredibly complex project” , it aims to transform the neoclassical building, which sits opposite the Royal Exchange and adjacent to the Mansion House, into what some staff hope is a Google-like workplace of friendly office spaces, breakout rooms and in-house cafes.

The Bank says there will be no delays, citing the appointment of architects last November. A project manager, a cost consultant and a firm of engineers were also signed up, and they have already begun evaluating budgets and timescales.

A Bank of England spokesperson said: “As part of our plans to preserve our historic Threadneedle Street office we are considering how best to renovate the site and optimise our running costs. All our procurement processes aim to deliver value for money.”

Bailey’s team – based in a grand part of the Bank known as the Parlours – will need to judge the cost implications of meeting new regulations on fire safety, accessibility, electrical testing – with the fire at Notre Dame mid-renovation still fresh in the memory – new plumbing and the need to have a more environmentally friendly building with heating based on renewable sources.

And that’s not to mention the security of the building while all this goes on. Bailey will be concerned that the 400,000 bars of gold, worth more than £200bn, and £100m of bank notes in the vaults are safe from terrorists and thieves.

A further complication is the fate of the Bank’s museum , which is now open to the public and tucked away in the side of the building, facing on to Bartholomew Lane.

Some senior staff had wanted to relocate the museum into the central quad and have the 100,000 visitors a year – mainly schoolchildren – march through the main entrance. Others wanted to have cafe space near the entrance to make the Bank appear more modern and appealing to visitors.

Vivienne Grafton, the executive director of central operations, told the Architects Journal: “This is an opportunity to breathe new life into a legacy building, not through radical reinvention, but through thoughtful, intelligent transformation.”

But architectural plans have yet to be agreed with the local authority – the City of London Corporation – and Historic England, which must sanction the proposed work on a building considered a cornerstone of Britain’s financial district.…

items.lbText:
About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users

At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined.

About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator .

In February 6.3% of households had someone using GLP-1 drugs, rising to 8.5% in August. Weight-loss pills such as Wegovy were approved in the UK in June. Patients previously had to use the injectable version.

Pills now account for more than one in 10 (11.2%) of GLP-1 users, while men are also driving the increase. Men make up just under a third (32%) of people taking weight-loss medication, up from 23% in February. Male users have nearly doubled to 830,000, up from 440,000 nine months ago.

The increased use of medications such as Mounjaro and Wegovy is causing people to buy less food at the supermarket and change their buying habits, according to a survey of more than 9,600 households.

In the year after starting to take the drugs, households with a GLP‑1 user collectively spent £1bn less on groceries than expected compared with similar households. In June, Worldpanel calculated the total saved by households with a GLP-1 user was £780m.

This represents 415m fewer items bought, or £389 a year displaced from the shopping baskets of households with a GLP-1 user, according to the research by Worldpanel, which has been tracking the effects of the drugs on buying behaviour since March 2024.

Nishita Pattni, a senior consultant for Worldpanel by Numerator, said: “In just six months, between February and August 2026, user numbers rose almost as much as they did in the whole of the previous year.

“For many people, a daily pill is far easier than an injection, and with the surge in male users, we only expect the appeal of these drugs to grow.”

GLP-1 users are now found in a similar percentage of households in Great Britain as those that buy popular branded products such as Kellogg’s Rice Krispies (8.6%) and Corona beer (8.4%).

People taking weight-loss medication were not simply buying fewer groceries, the research found. Spend and volume were falling at a similar rate, creating winners and losers.

Products associated with indulgence, as well as impulse purchases, have taken the biggest hit.

Alcohol spend has fallen by 15% more among GLP-1 users than in households where no one uses GLP-1, while the spend on crisps has fallen by a similar percentage, as users tend to snack less.

Conversely, portion-controlled products are growing in popularity. There has been a 30% rise in the number of frozen ready-meals sold, and an increase in the volume and spend on hot chocolate and malt drinks as people who take weight-loss drugs continue to enjoy small treats.

Chantel Kennaugh, the head of public sector and nutrition for Worldpanel by Numerator, said estimates suggest that GLP-1 usage is likely to surpass 10% of households in Great Britain in 2027. “This is not a flash-in-the-pan trend, but a seismic change that requires retailers and manufacturers to rethink their strategies.”

items.lbText:
Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan’s government could be about to lift a ban on imported American potatoes, which famers say would threaten their livelihoods

It could be a piping hot croquette eaten on the go, a bowl of nikujaga stew or a plate of home-cooked chips. One culinary thread runs through them all – the Japanese potato.

Along with rice , the crop is fiercely protected as one of only a few homegrown staples in a country that imports more than 60% of its food.

But that could be about to change. Under pressure from Donald Trump , Japan is moving towards lifting a 76-year-old ban on imported American potatoes .

Japan’s potato farmers say lifting the ban would threaten their livelihoods, and expose consumers to an inferior product. They worry batches of American potatoes could bring harmful insects and pests into Japanese fields.

Tokyo partially lifted the ban in 2006 to permit imports of US potatoes exclusively to make crisps. The vegetables must be transported in sealed containers and then cooked at a high temperature to prevent the spread of pests and diseases.

But a complete lifting of the ban would put fresh American potatoes on restaurant menus and supermarket shelves for the first time since 1950.

“We have repeatedly and unequivocally stated our opposition to imports,” said Toshihide Numasawa, an employee of the Japan Agriculture group in Hokkaido, where about 80% of the country’s potatoes are grown. He said there were various reasons for the objection, including the “risk of pests and diseases entering the country and damage to Hokkaido’s production areas.”

Potatoes were initially collector’s items for intrigued plant enthusiasts when Dutch traders introduced them to Japan in 1598. By the mid-1800s, potatoes were a nutritious alternative to rice – a crop unsuited to Hokkaido’s cooler climate. Now they are the basis for the perennial favourite jaga bata , a baked version slathered in butter, while poteto sarada has practically achieved national-dish status.

Hokkaido’s best-known variety is the Danshaku (Irish Cobbler), a potato high in starch whose fluffy, absorbent flesh makes them perfect for butter and other toppings or to soak up meat juices in a stew.

“We believe consumers have come to recognise which are best suited to particular dishes,” said Numasawa, adding that Hokkaido potato farmers were also being buffeted by homegrown pest outbreaks, global heating and rural depopulation.

The country now grows more than 90 varieties of potato and Japanese consumers ate 3.5m tons of potatoes in 2024, according to the agriculture ministry, among them 1.2m tons of fresh imports used to make crisps.

The tuber’s place at the centre of Japan-US trade negotiations has created an early headache for Japan’s new agriculture minister, Arata Takebe, whose constituency is located in prime potato-growing country in Hokkaido.

The plan to lift the ban “should progress after thorough scientific and technical discussion” Takebe recently told Jiji Press, adding that a decision could take “considerable time”.

“I know the [US] side has strong expectations, but the ban on imports will not be lifted without sufficient discussions or an agreement acceptable to both sides,” he said.

While potatoes imported for crisps are subject to strict quarantine measures, farmers fear batches of imported fresh potatoes could bring in harmful insects and microbes. Japan’s government has identified 21 pests and diseases that could pose a risk of invasion.

The potato cyst nematode and pale potato cyst nematode are causing most concern. Although they are not a threat to human health, they can damage the vegetable’s roots, which stunts their growth, and remain present in soil for more than 15 years.

Earlier this year, congressional lawmakers urged Trump to continue raising the ban with the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.

“US potato growers produce the best potatoes in the world,” they wrote in a letter. “Japan represents a massive market with significant export opportunities for American potato growers.”

After raising the issue during his first term in office, Trump has persuaded Japan’s government to begin talks as he faces accusations that his policies have been “ disastrous ” for rural America.

Supporters of lifting the ban say it would lower prices for Japanese consumers and bring American farmers an additional $150m a year in export earnings.

But farmers in Hokkaido claim that not enough has been done to eliminate the threat from pests and disease.

“Protecting Hokkaido’s agriculture is not just about protecting Hokkaido,” the Hokkaido Agricultural Corporations Association said in a statement. “It also means protecting the production base that will support Japan’s food supply for the future.”

Naohiro Makino, a potato farmer in Hokkaido, said the ban on fresh potatoes should stay. “Once pests get in, you can’t grow potatoes for more than a decade,” he told the Asahi Shimbun newspaper. “For the sake of the farmland our ancestors protected, I am firmly opposed [to lifting the ban].”

Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial

When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country.

The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence.

Then he came across Project Search, a nationwide year-long transition-to-work programme that helps young people with learning disabilities or autism move into permanent paid employment.

It changed his life and now Bowman is thriving in his work as a personal trainer at Pure Gym.

“Getting actual experience in workplaces, understanding how they function, what would be expected of me and how to interact with people, it was exactly what I needed,” he said. “And having a job coach who does half the jump with you.”

Alan Milburn’s report on how to get the UK’s Neets into work has recommended an overhaul of welfare support for young people , including moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits and on to a new “youth allowance”.

In return, eligible 18-to-24-year-olds will be guaranteed a fully funded, six-month job if they have been claiming universal credit for 12 months. Milburn said this was about prioritising “their longer-term life chances” over “immediate shorter-term finances”.

Interns and staff at the Project Search course run by Phoenix College in Tower Hamlets welcomed the bold commitment to get more young people into work, but there were concerns about cutting support and the quality of job opportunities being offered.

Bowman said he disagreed with the proposal to cut benefits like the personal independence payment (Pip) for young people to help push them into work.

“I think alongside any workplace initiatives, Pip is still absolutely a must-have. I would argue it’s more important to have if you’re going to be engaging in a structured programme – for me, things like noise-cancelling headphones are essential,” he said.

“I need that funding more to enter the world of work than I did when I was sat at home playing video games.”

Staff said getting young people, especially those with extra needs, into a long-term sustainable job wasn’t as simple as filling a vacancy – many students need holistic support and extra help even once they’re in work.

“We’ve been noticing a lot more interns coming in with serious mental health conditions and that requires extra help,” said Renato Marques, principal of Phoenix College. “But here, even for our very high-needs students, everything is geared towards getting them into a workplace.

“They learn the job doing the job. A lot of courses say they are preparing students for work, but they are not taking them into work.”

Rather than studying at a traditional campus, their interns learn in classrooms hosted in partner businesses – including a global law firm, a large distribution company and Queen Mary University of London – and they rotate through daily 9am to 3pm work placements.

Over the past six years, 68% of students ended up in employment at the end of the course – four times higher than the national average rate of disabled young people who are Neet.

All graduates also have access to a follow-on service they can use for advice in the first few years of their career.

For students with higher levels of need, the college developed a pre-supported internship combining two days of workplace experience – supported by an on-hand job coach – with extra training in social skills and independent travel.

Osman Osman, assistant principal for Project Search, said Milburn’s plan would only work with better paid and resourced careers advisers in schools, and high-quality work experience and job offers.

“You see careers advisers managing schools with a thousand kids, and they’re expected to meet with every single one, and it’s a very, very hard job to actually get those young people work-ready,” he said. “We spend a long time building our young people’s confidence and skillset in the field they’re interested in.

“And any job offer has to be meaningful placements because inset days, taster sessions or a week’s work experience often lead to no actual outcomes for young people.”

Tawhid Ahmed, 21, said finding work or apprenticeships after finishing school had been overwhelming – he now works at Phoenix College after building confidence and social skills on the course.

“I have a learning disability, and it was hard because I’ve been rejected for so many jobs. The fact that I was able to find Project Search really was a blessing,” he said. “Now I do admin and I have really good colleagues who help and support me. I want to help students face challenges that I’ve faced as well.”

Businesses are also a key part of the puzzle – Milburn’s proposals included a raft of incentives to encourage employers to take on more young people, including tax breaks.

“Employers might scoff at the review because there’s a lot of expectations placed on them,” said Cigdem Yilmaz, supported employment lead on the course. “We need an army of people, maybe that’s people like us, to be working with employers until we can get more young people on to the ground. Otherwise it’s just going to be more of the same.”

Max, a 22-year-old with autism, is being supported by the Youth Environmental Service (Yes), which works with environmental organisations to create accessible and entry-level employment in the west of England.

The organisation, which targets young people from diverse backgrounds and those with disabilities, provides access to paid work as well as peer support networks, a transferable skills programme and one-to-one coaching.…

Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

O n Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider , which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset .

“Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director.

One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says.

The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.”

The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.”

He is trying to use fewer pesticides, so is keen to find varieties that are naturally resistant to disease and pests, and will blossom at exactly the moment when spring conditions suit apple tree pollinators such as bumblebees and honeybees.

Another priority is to find varieties that need less winter chill in a warming climate: apple trees, he explains, need a sustained cold period in winter to complete their dormancy, which enables their fruit buds to develop properly in spring. “That winter chill is really important – and last year, we probably didn’t have quite enough, and some varieties are more susceptible to a lack of winter chill than others.”

Thatchers’ orchard manager, Chris Muntz Torres, says jonagold, a cross between golden delicious and a jonathan apple, performed particularly well in trials this year. “They’ve got this vigour, this willingness to grow, whatever the weather.”

He thinks this is because the tree’s vigorous growth above ground is matched by a strong root system. “That’s what we want – a variety that, irrespective of the weather, is robust enough to grow.”

Myrtle Farm has also begun planting wildflower strips in its orchards, to attract insects that prey on pests such as the rosy apple aphid – a strategy that research has shown could save apple growers up to £3,000 a hectare every year and support native pollinators.

Nigel Jenner, head of agronomy for tree fruit at the global fruit producer AM Fresh UK, works with independent apple farmers, who represent about 30% of Britain’s apple-growing industry. He says roughly 70% of these growers – about 220 – have planted wildflower strips in the past five years, and that number is increasing.

“We know this is the way forward,” Jenner says. “It works and it has a meaningful effect on your chemical input and your spray bill.”

He hopes seed producers will soon develop an “orchard mix” of wildflowers designed to attract the beneficial insects that apple growers need, and produce enough of it to bring prices down and make the practice even more widespread.

Many independent growers are also experimenting with new methods of water management, Jenner says. “Years ago, you’d kick the soil and say ‘oh that’s a bit dry, we’ll water it’. Now, we’re using neutron probes to measure the water deficit and we’re trying to get the trees to hunt for water.”

This involves letting the trees become water-stressed, he says: the top 65mm of soil in an orchard is left to dry out, which encourages deeper root growth and reduces the need for irrigation.

Back at Myrtle Farm, Thatchers is also working to improve soil health through regenerative farming. Before any trees are planted in new orchards, herbal leys – mixtures of grasses, legumes and deep-rooted herbs such as chicory – are sown and the land is grazed by sheep.

“Their little feet pound the ground, which improves the soil structure, and they eat the herbal ley and then recycle it very effectively back into the ground, which also improves the soil structure. So where we’ve had fields that have been continuous cereals or maize, we’ve found that within three years, the soil on all the metrics that are important for growing apples improves by at least 20%,” says Thatcher.…
